routes.description: Establish that human freedom requires genuinely live alternatives and agent sourcehood, and that deliberative experience, constrained indeterminacy, executive selection, and cumulative self-formation can jointly supply those conditions despite biological and social limits.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if alternative-capable deliberation and agent contribution are necessary for freedom and responsibility, if indeterminism can operate through rather than replace rational selection, and if deterministic proximal agency cannot preserve the required authorship.

motionBridge.description: Show that freedom requires both genuinely available alternatives and an agent-originating contribution that deterministic practical agency cannot supply.

centralBridges.description: Establish that first-person deliberation and practical inquiry present alternatives as genuinely available rather than merely hypothetical.
Explain how constrained neural indeterminacy and executive criteria permit rational selection without reducing choice to either prior determination or randomness.
Show that agents originate action and progressively shape their own characters through repeated alternative-capable choices under inherited constraints.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Establish that neuroscience does not decisively show conscious deliberation to be causally idle or choices to be settled before awareness.
Provide a non-dualist account on which conscious valition, brain-level realization, top-down constraint, and indeterminacy can belong to one agent.

routes.description: Establish that determinism preserves practically important freedom through willing action, consent, proximal causation, character, and responsibility practices, without requiring categorical alternatives or ultimate self-origination.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if meaningful distinctions between choices and nonchoices remain available under determinism, if persons can act through their brains and characters as proximal sources, and if libertarian alternatives or sourcehood add no necessary, workable condition for responsibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that freedom, will, and responsibility retain burden-satisfying practical content under determinism without libertarian alternatives or ultimate sourcehood.

centralBridges.description: Ground freedom in durable distinctions among willing, unwilling, consensual, coerced, chosen, and unchosen conduct.
Show that an embodied person can be the causally effective proximal source of conduct through deliberation and character even when prior conditions determine it.
Explain responsibility through plural, practice-shaped concepts of praise, blame, answerability, and reactive attitudes rather than one libertarian essence.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether genetics, upbringing, and restricted evaluative criteria leave libertarian agents with the ultimate authorship their account requires.
Require a principled account of when an alternative is genuinely live and how that status explains responsibility across constrained cases.

sections.title: The Required Standard of Human Freedom
sections.rationale: Defines the motion-level dispute between libertarian alternatives and sourcehood on one side and compatibilist willing, choice, and practical agency on the other.

sections.title: Deliberation and Genuine Alternative Possibilities
sections.rationale: Tests whether first-person deliberation and practical inquiry support genuinely open options or can coexist with a determined future understood from a third-person perspective.

sections.title: Indeterminism, Randomness, and Agential Selection
sections.rationale: Addresses whether constrained stochastic variation plus executive criteria can produce rational libertarian choice, or whether probabilistic weighting still fails to confer authorship.

sections.title: Sourcehood, Character, and Formative Constraints
sections.rationale: Compares cumulative libertarian self-formation with compatibilist proximal causation while accounting for the roles of genetics, upbringing, evaluative criteria, and constrained opportunities.

sections.title: Responsibility and Practical Agency Under Determinism
sections.rationale: Examines whether consent, coercion, willing conduct, blame, praise, and reactive attitudes preserve freedom-relevant distinctions without categorical alternatives or ultimate sourcehood.

routes.description: Establish that a revisable naturalist epistemology integrates scientific knowledge without requiring a supernatural layer, accounts for the named scientific domains within a rule-governed physical picture, and supports humanly grounded morality and meaning.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if naturalism supplies coherent treatments of cosmology, fine-tuning, quantum mechanics, consciousness, agency, morality, and meaning while showing that theistic additions are unnecessary or generate expectations not borne out by the world.

motionBridge.description: Connect scientific explanations and human normative practices into a coherent naturalist worldview that addresses every principal domain named in the motion.

centralBridges.description: Show that fallible, empirically checked inquiry warrants a unified natural order without claiming that every scientific or philosophical question is settled.
Explain why self-contained cosmology and naturalistic selection mechanisms can address cosmic origins and apparent fine-tuning without design.
Show that quantum theory, emergent agency, and an unfinished neuroscience of consciousness remain compatible with physicalism.
Ground morality, plural value, and finite-life meaning in human judgments, relationships, and practices without an external moral lawgiver.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test theism against expectations concerning revelation, suffering, religious diversity, miracles, and the observed scale and character of the universe.
Explain how naturalists may retain moral insights and community-relevant resources from religious traditions without accepting supernatural authority.

routes.description: Establish that responsible theism can integrate scientific knowledge by distinguishing established findings from metaphysical interpretation, allowing science to correct religious understandings while retaining rational commitments to divine purpose, moral order, and transcendent hope.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if scientific accounts are shown not to compel naturalism, theistic belief remains rational under responsible reexamination, and theism supplies coherent treatments of creation, persons, morality, suffering, vocation, and meaning.

motionBridge.description: Connect scientifically responsible inquiry with a theistic metaphysics that remains open to correction while addressing every principal domain named in the motion.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish empirical findings from optional metaphysical glosses and specify how established science may correct historically situated religious interpretation.
Show that complete physical mechanisms for cosmic origins and qualified fine-tuning claims remain compatible with divine creation and purpose.
Establish that quantum mechanics, physical accounts of mentality, and scientific uncertainty do not uniquely settle metaphysics, personhood, or agency.
Connect theism to a real moral order, responsible engagement with suffering, present-life vocation, and hope beyond finitude.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why divine freedom, human discovery, and historically mediated revelation need not make scripture a source of detailed scientific results.
Show how inherited theistic commitments may remain rational when periodically reexamined and when apparent defeaters receive responsible consideration.

sections.title: Scientific Knowledge, Revelation, and Worldview Method
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the governing standards for integrating empirical inquiry with naturalist or theistic commitments, including revisability, rational belief maintenance, revelation, and the distinction between scientific findings and metaphysical interpretation.

sections.title: Cosmic Origins, Contingency, and Fine-Tuning
sections.rationale: Cosmology and fine-tuning provide the debate's main test of whether physical self-containment and observer selection remove an explanatory role for God or remain compatible with divine creation and purpose.

sections.title: Quantum Mechanics, Metaphysical Underdetermination, and Agency
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether quantum theory carries consequences for materialism, logic, determinism, and free will, and whether emergent agency or interpretive underdetermination best connects physics to metaphysics.

sections.title: Consciousness, Physicalism, and Personhood
sections.rationale: Consciousness and the status of persons form a direct test of physical reduction, emergent explanation, non-naturalist openness, and the limits of conclusions that may presently be drawn from neuroscience or mathematical modeling.

sections.title: Morality, Suffering, Meaning, and Human Vocation
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of moral order, humanly constructed value, evil, finite life, afterlife, plural callings, and existential meaning determine how each metaphysical picture addresses the motion beyond fundamental physics.

routes.description: Establish that the West’s transformation toward universal concern is genuine moral progress by distinguishing changing applications from enduring moral principles and arguing that obligations, human dignity, moral comparison, and guilt require an objective standard grounded beyond evolved preference.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if shared moral principles and the normative features of obligation, progress, condemnation, and guilt are shown to require a mind-independent standard, and if Jesus’s expansion of concern is coherently explained as fuller recognition or application of that standard.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus’s historically transformative teaching points to genuine moral truth and progress rather than merely a change in prevailing inclination.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish enduring cross-cultural moral principles from historically variable practices and expansions of their scope.
Explain why obligations and rankings among conflicting inclinations require authority beyond contingently evolved feelings or preferences.
Connect objective human value and moral duties to grounding beyond humanity, including the account of persons as bearing God’s image.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend access to immaterial moral truth by distinguishing moral inquiry from the methods appropriate to physical science and history.
Use guilt and the perceived need for forgiveness as phenomena requiring comparison between realist and inclination-based explanations.

routes.description: Explain Western moral transformation as Jesus’s historically distinctive universalization of evolved and socially inherited concern, while arguing that human moral judgment, motivation, and practice can be grounded in constitutive inclinations without accessible objective values or divine grounding.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if historical variation and subjective epistemic access undercut the inference to objective morality, while evolved human nature and historically developed commitments adequately explain moral conviction, action, guilt, and the emergence of universal charity.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus’s influence can explain a major historical change in Western moral inclination without establishing objective or divinely grounded moral truth.

centralBridges.description: Establish that universal concern for unrelated needy people emerged historically and was not a constant feature of human moral practice.
Show how deeply rooted human nature and evolved inclinations can ground moral belief, motivation, and action without an external standard.
Explain why cognition through subjective human minds and persistent moral diversity limit any claimed access to objective moral values.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide evolutionary accounts of altruistic dispositions and guilt that do not presuppose a real moral code.
Separate the historical account of Jesus’s ethical influence from the further metaethical claim that the resulting values are objective.

sections.title: Objective Truth and Human Access
sections.rationale: The debate requires both sides to address whether mind-independent moral truth can exist and be known despite every judgment being formed through human cognitive faculties.

sections.title: Cross-Cultural Commonality and Historical Variation
sections.rationale: Claims about shared principles and divergent practices determine whether the historical record supports enduring moral truth or historically contingent human morality.

sections.title: Jesus and the Universalization of Charity
sections.rationale: The scope and meaning of Jesus’s extension of care beyond kin and social groups connects the agreed historical transformation directly to the competing explanations named in the motion.

sections.title: Inclination, Obligation, and Moral Progress
sections.rationale: The central normative clash is whether evolved inclinations can ground duties and comparisons among competing impulses or whether genuine obligation and progress require an objective standard.

sections.title: Guilt, Moral Practice, and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: Competing explanations of guilt, moral action, condemnation, and the transformation itself test how much each account explains beyond the historical facts both sides substantially accept.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity distinctively transformed inherited ideas into universal dignity, equality, bodily integrity, and moral concern, then trace modern Western rights, reform, humanism, science, and secular institutions through that Christian conceptual inheritance.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if it connects distinctive Christian moral mechanisms to enduring Western concepts and institutions while explaining why classical borrowings, historical failures, and nominally secular reform do not break the claimed genealogy.

motionBridge.description: Show that the modern West's defining human values depend principally on distinctive Christian transformations and their continuing cultural transmission.

centralBridges.description: Explain how the crucified victim, universal divine kinship, and humanity's divine image generate exceptional and equal human dignity.
Connect Christian universalism to consequential changes in slavery, sexual power, bodily integrity, marriage, rights, and reform.
Demonstrate that Renaissance, science, Enlightenment, humanism, and secularism developed through Christian institutions or conceptual patterns rather than independently of them.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Christianity's reconfiguration of earlier materials from mere repetition or passive borrowing.
Account for Christianity's preservation and transmission of classical learning despite disputes about suppression and delay.

routes.description: Establish that Western human values and intellectual modernity have substantial pre-Christian and non-Christian sources, while showing that Christian borrowing, institutional conduct, and delayed reform weaken the claim to distinctive or primary causal credit.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if classical, Axial Age, cross-cultural, Enlightenment, and secular sources adequately explain dignity, equality, humanism, science, and moral concern without requiring Christianity as their principal origin.

motionBridge.description: Show that modern Western human values owe more to older, plural, rational, and secular traditions than to a uniquely Christian inheritance.

centralBridges.description: Trace equality, cosmopolitan obligation, natural liberty, friendship, and ethical reflection to Axial Age and classical traditions.
Establish that shared humanity, compassion, and humanistic ethics arose independently across multiple pre-Christian and non-Christian cultures.
Connect Renaissance recovery, empirical science, Enlightenment reason, and secular humanism to freedom from inherited ecclesiastical authority.
Test Christian causal claims against borrowing, cultural suppression, misogyny, slavery, delayed reform, and contested claims of novelty.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Recognize Arab, Persian, monastic, and other channels in the preservation and transmission of classical knowledge.
Require claimed Christian contributions to be both historically distinctive and materially explanatory of the values at issue.

sections.title: Origins of Universal Dignity and Equality
sections.rationale: This issue tests the central genealogical dispute between Christian moral reversal and divine-image doctrines on one side and Stoic, Axial Age, and other pre-Christian accounts of universality on the other.

sections.title: Humanism, Compassion, and Cross-Cultural Parallels
sections.rationale: The geographic and historical independence of humanistic concern determines whether modern humanism requires Christian cultural inheritance or can arise through reflection on shared humanity.

sections.title: Slavery, Gender, Bodily Integrity, and Reform
sections.rationale: Concrete disputes over slavery, sexual power, gender, marriage, and abolition test whether Christian universalism produced durable moral change or coexisted with practices inconsistent with that genealogy.

sections.title: Classical Borrowing, Suppression, and Preservation
sections.rationale: The relationship between Christianity and classical culture bears on whether Christianity transformed and transmitted prior sources or depended upon, suppressed, and only later recovered them.

sections.title: Science, Enlightenment, Rights, and Secularism
sections.rationale: Competing explanations of universities, scientific inquiry, Enlightenment rights, secularism, and modern humanism determine whether intellectual modernity continues Christian patterns or represents recovery and emancipation from ecclesiastical authority.

routes.description: Establish that a consciously willing first cause is conceptually required, that this conclusion may be grounded as a self-evident axiom rather than an unsupported presupposition, and that experiential, testimonial, or historical considerations can supplement that foundation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the need for an ultimate cause is connected to conscious agency, its axiomatic status is justified without merely assuming the conclusion, and the resulting framework supplies burden-relevant support for God rather than only criticizing skepticism.

motionBridge.description: Show that the axiomatic and supplementary considerations provide good evidence for God rather than merely an asserted epistemic starting point.

centralBridges.description: Establish that causal regress must terminate in an ultimate cause whose initiation of derivative causes entails conscious will.
Establish that the divine first cause is conceptually ineliminable and self-evident, distinguishing an axiom from an unsupported presupposition.
Connect the epistemic foundation to identifiable support for divine existence or activity, including miracle, historical, testimonial, or experiential considerations.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show why sensitivity-based religious skepticism cannot impose an exhaustive verification requirement without undermining closure and ordinary inference.
Define whether the argument supports generic theism, monotheism, or a specifically Christian conclusion and explain any narrowing principle.

routes.description: Require publicly assessable support that distinguishes God from rival explanations, test whether the first-cause and axiomatic claims meet that standard, and examine whether miracle, testimony, experience, or scripture supplies the missing connection to divine causation.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative considerations remain assumptions, methods, or reports without a demonstrated and discriminating evidential connection to God, while the burden stays with the party asserting divine existence.

motionBridge.description: Show that the offered case does not provide good evidence connecting observable or inferential grounds to God and cannot satisfy the motion through axiomatic assertion alone.

centralBridges.description: Specify a fallible evidential standard requiring facts, explanatory fit, and discrimination among comparably compatible rival explanations.
Test the infinite-past premise, the extension of time and causality beyond the universe, and the inference from an ultimate cause to conscious divine will.
Show why naming God as an axiom does not itself furnish an argument or distinguish theism from incompatible axiomatic starting points.
Require detectable divine action to be supported by an assessable connection between the reported phenomenon and divine causation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Maintain that failure to disprove God does not replace the affirmative obligation to provide positive support for belief.
Test whether testimony, private experience, resurrection claims, and scriptural interpretation are handled under shared and consistently applied evidential standards.

sections.title: Epistemic burden and the standard for good evidence
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether warranted belief requires certainty, what makes a method evidentially discriminating, and whether criticizing skepticism can contribute to the affirmative burden without positive support for God.

sections.title: First cause, temporal regress, and conscious will
sections.rationale: This is the principal positive route from the existence of a causal order to an ultimate foundation and then to divine agency, encompassing disputes about infinite regress, atemporality, necessity, and conscious initiation.

sections.title: Axiomatic necessity or unsupported assumption
sections.rationale: The debate centrally turns on whether conceptual ineliminability and self-evidence can make God an evidential axiom, or whether the same procedure permits incompatible starting points without a means of adjudication.

sections.title: Miracles, testimony, and personal experience
sections.rationale: This issue tests the transition from an abstract epistemic framework to claimed manifestations of God, including whether resurrection testimony, miracle reports, and private experience can be identified and attributed to divine action.

sections.title: Scope and consistency of theistic and scriptural evidence
sections.rationale: This issue addresses how far the offered reasoning reaches and whether parsimony, scriptural accuracy, and literal or figurative interpretation consistently narrow generic first-cause reasoning toward a particular theistic framework.

routes.description: Establish that empirical inquiry has genuine domain limits, that rational guidance may include probabilistic and faith-informed inference about existential and moral questions, and that conservative institutions and market mechanisms can translate such guidance into social policy.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by connecting the limits of empirical access to a warranted role for nonempirical inference, then showing how objective human features, inherited institutions, voluntary exchange, and incentive-sensitive policy can guide contested questions without requiring empirical certainty.

motionBridge.description: Show that faith-informed inference and conservative consequences can legitimately guide belief and policy where empirical methods underdetermine existential, moral, or institutional questions.

centralBridges.description: Establish that unresolved questions about origins, purpose, morality, and postmortem existence are not exhausted by present empirical inquiry.
Explain when probabilistic reasoning, practical uncertainty, or high-stakes consequences warrant attention to possibilities lacking direct verification.
Connect biological or moral features of human beings to social norms and institutions that are claimed to track those features.
Show how voluntary exchange, dispersed information, competition, and cost awareness can guide welfare policy and justify unequal outcomes.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Identify incentive structures or institutional interests that may complicate reliance on expert consensus or government-administered systems.
Explain why longstanding sex-based or conscience-sensitive arrangements may serve protective purposes that proposed reforms must address.

routes.description: Establish that belief should remain proportionate to publicly accessible evidence, that unsupported supernatural claims retain their burden of proof, and that political and social arrangements should be judged by secular-humanist consequences for autonomy, health, and shared welfare.
routes.successCriteria: The route is completed by distinguishing uncertainty from affirmative unsupported belief, defending empirical correction and relevant expertise, and applying evidence about harm and well-being to religion in public institutions, gender policy, labor, and health care.

motionBridge.description: Show that empirical warrant and secular-humanist consequences provide the appropriate standards for beliefs and policies affecting other people.

centralBridges.description: Require confidence and inference to remain proportionate to available evidence while assigning affirmative supernatural claims their burden of proof.
Defend scientific evidence, relevant expertise, and revisability as the governing means of resolving factual disputes about the natural and social world.
Connect personal autonomy and religious neutrality to the treatment of identity, legislation, and essential public-facing institutions.
Assess markets, wages, health care, and public policy by their consequences for preventable harm, reciprocal dependence, and access to basic goods.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Show why high stakes or imaginable possibilities do not select one religious conclusion when incompatible alternatives remain evidentially unresolved.
Develop measurable, harm-sensitive alternatives where inherited classifications or consumer-market analogies fail to capture relevant human needs.

sections.title: Evidence, uncertainty, and faith-informed inference
sections.rationale: This issue supplies the governing standards for the entire motion: the burden of supernatural claims, the limits of empirical access, proportional confidence, probabilistic inference, and whether practical stakes can warrant belief or action under uncertainty.

sections.title: Scientific authority, correction, and institutional incentives
sections.rationale: This section tests how each route handles contested natural-world claims by examining empirical inference, scientific revisability, expert reliance, funding incentives, and the separation of observed mechanisms from causal or policy conclusions.

sections.title: Gender, human nature, autonomy, and public institutions
sections.rationale: The gender and religious-neutrality disputes apply the competing standards to biological facts, socially constructed identity, welfare evidence, protective institutions, personal conscience, and the obligations of government and community-serving organizations.

sections.title: Markets, inequality, labor, and human welfare
sections.rationale: This issue contrasts voluntary exchange and entrepreneurial value with living-wage and distributional concerns, clarifying whether market consent or broader effects on workers and society should govern political-economic judgments.

sections.title: Health-care access, incentives, and reciprocal social dependence
sections.rationale: Health care provides a concrete policy test of consumer choice, third-party payment, public mandates, professional expertise, preventable suffering, and the extent to which shared welfare creates collective obligations.

routes.description: Establish that contingency, a finite cosmic past, life-permitting fine-tuning, objective morality, and the historical case for Jesus's resurrection collectively raise the probability of God's existence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cited facts are sufficiently established, are more expected or better explained given theism than its relevant alternatives, and cumulatively support the motion's evidentiary threshold.

motionBridge.description: The motion is satisfied if the cumulative considerations make God's existence more probable than it would otherwise be.

centralBridges.description: Contingent reality and a universe with a finite past must warrant inference to a necessary, transcendent causal ground.
Life-permitting constants and initial conditions must be better explained by design than by necessity, chance, or multiverse selection.
Objective moral values and duties must exist and require an ontological foundation supplied by God's necessary moral nature.
The relevant historical facts concerning Jesus must be established and better explained by divine resurrection than by naturalistic alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Philosophical, moral, historical, and scientific considerations must be admissible within a probability-raising conception of evidence.
The several independent considerations must retain material cumulative force even if no individual consideration proves theism by itself.

routes.description: Show that the affirmative considerations are unsupported, underdetermined, or more plausibly addressed through empirical naturalism, so they do not supply adequate evidence for a divine cause or the Christian God.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the affirmative fails to justify its probability assignments or if natural models, explanatory uncertainty, secular morality, and ordinary historical explanations prevent the cited facts from discriminating in favor of God.

motionBridge.description: The motion is not established unless the affirmative supplies testable or otherwise warranted evidence that favors God over relevant natural alternatives.

centralBridges.description: Quantum-gravity, multiverse, or other physical possibilities must block the inference from contingency or cosmic beginnings to a uniquely divine cause.
Dynamical explanations and observer selection must make apparent fine-tuning insufficient to distinguish purposive design from natural cosmology.
Moral truth or understanding must remain intelligible without divine grounding, or the proposed divine foundation must face an unresolved arbitrariness problem.
Human error, illusion, imagination, or intervention must remain more plausible than resurrection as explanations of the reported historical claims.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Claims about divine evidence must meet a defensible empirical or probabilistic standard rather than rest on intuition or unquantified priors.
Present explanatory ignorance must remain a reason for continued investigation rather than an evidential inference to supernatural agency.

sections.title: Evidential Standards and the Cumulative Inference
sections.rationale: The parties dispute what qualifies as evidence, how probability-raising claims are warranted, where the burden lies, and whether several distinct considerations can jointly support the motion.

sections.title: Contingency and the Necessary Explanatory Ground
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether contingent reality requires an external necessary explanation and whether God has any justified advantage over a necessary or eternal natural terminus.

sections.title: Cosmic Beginning, Infinity, and Transcendent Causation
sections.rationale: The finite-past argument depends on philosophical claims about actual infinity, scientific claims about cosmic boundaries, and the inference from a beginning to a transcendent cause.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Design, and Multiverse Selection
sections.rationale: This section addresses whether life-permitting conditions favor purposive design or are better treated through dynamics, varied universes, observer selection, and unresolved physical theory.

sections.title: Moral Objectivity and Divine Grounding
sections.rationale: The moral argument requires both objective values or duties and a uniquely divine ontology, while the opposing route contests that dependence through rational, biological, and arbitrariness-based alternatives.

sections.title: Resurrection and Competing Historical Explanations
sections.rationale: The historical pillar turns on the status of the alleged facts, their connection to God's existence, and the comparative plausibility of resurrection against ordinary human explanations.

routes.description: Establish that a first-century Jewish preacher existed behind the Christian traditions by combining early Pauline testimony, multiple source traditions, historically plausible context, and the distinction between legendary development and personal nonexistence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if independent and comparatively early evidence is more probable given an earthly Jesus than a wholly mythical origin, while source criticism can reject legendary details without eliminating the underlying person.

motionBridge.description: Show that the cumulative source pattern makes a historical Jewish person behind the traditions more probable than an origin without such a person.

centralBridges.description: Establish that early Pauline material refers to an earthly Jewish Jesus and connects Paul with people represented as Jesus's brother and disciple.
Establish that multiple comparatively early traditions provide historically significant attestation rather than merely repeating one late narrative.
Explain why proclamation of a crucified Messiah is more expected as a response to an actual execution than as an invention from prevailing Jewish expectations.
Show that mythic, miraculous, or scripturally patterned accretions can surround a person whose existence remains historically recoverable.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Prefer explanations grounded in first-century Jewish and Roman conditions over proposed analogies whose relevant evidence is culturally remote or later.
Apply comparative historical probability through source proximity, independence, contextual fit, and explanatory economy.

routes.description: Establish that Christianity can be explained without a recoverable first-century preacher by challenging the independence, authenticity, and terrestrial meaning of the sources while offering celestial, scriptural, and literary pathways for the development of Jesus traditions.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if purported historical anchors remain dependent, ambiguous, interpolated, or methodologically circular and the emergence of the exalted Christ is at least as well explained by mythic and scriptural development as by an ordinary founder.

motionBridge.description: Show that the surviving evidence does not require a historical preacher and remains compatible with Christianity developing without such a person.

centralBridges.description: Interpret the earliest Pauline Christ as accessible through revelation and scripture and as compatible with a celestial death followed by later historicization.
Show that Gospel sources, oral traditions, and external notices do not constitute securely independent attestations of an underlying person.
Provide a plausible pathway from Jewish divine, scriptural, or mythic materials to terrestrial narratives about Jesus.
Show that positing an ordinary teacher does not by itself explain the emergence and character of the exalted miracle-working Christ.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Preserve material uncertainty about historicizing passages through interpolation arguments, manuscript gaps, and disputed authorship.
Challenge historical reconstructions whose chronology, narrative anchors, or organizing paradigms presuppose the person they are meant to establish.

sections.title: Historical Method and Comparative Burden
sections.rationale: Defines the probability standard for the motion and tests how source proximity, independence, background knowledge, and competing explanatory paradigms bear on existence.

sections.title: Pauline Jesus and Textual Foundations
sections.rationale: Addresses the earliest principal evidence, including earthly or celestial reference, biographical silence, revelation, associates, interpolation, authorship, and textual authenticity.

sections.title: Gospel Traditions and Historical Recovery
sections.rationale: Tests whether multiple Gospel traditions preserve recoverable information about a person or instead reflect dependent literary, scriptural, and legendary construction.

sections.title: External Attestation and Chronology
sections.rationale: Examines whether non-Christian notices, ancient critics, oral transmission, and proposed early sources independently anchor Jesus or merely attest later Christian claims.

sections.title: Movement Origins, Jewish Context, and the Crucified Messiah
sections.rationale: Compares an executed Jewish founder followed by resurrection belief with celestial, theophanic, or scriptural origin models and asks which better explains the movement's emergence.

sections.title: Legendary Development and Explanatory Fit
sections.rationale: Determines whether mythic accretions are compatible with an underlying person and whether a minimal historical figure or a mythic origin better accounts for the resulting Christ traditions.

routes.description: Establish that transcendental facts require an adequate metaphysical ground and that a necessary personal mind explains their character and rational applicability better than the available non-theistic alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the need for grounding is established, impersonal and naturalistic accounts are comparatively inadequate, a necessary personal mind provides the relevant explanation, and philosophical or abductive support qualifies as good evidence for that conclusion.

motionBridge.description: Show that transcendental facts make a necessary personal God sufficiently better supported to constitute good evidence for the motion.

centralBridges.description: Establish that the necessity, objectivity, and applicability of transcendental facts call for an explanation beyond their practical use or description.
Connect the abstract and necessary character of transcendental facts to a necessary transcendent mind capable of grounding them.
Show that the divine account has greater explanatory adequacy than naturalism, Platonism, brute fact, or unspecified alternatives.
Establish that deductive and abductive philosophical reasoning can warrant the grounding inference without requiring exclusively empirical confirmation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain how a unified necessary ground can satisfy parsimony and explanatory-scope requirements.
Specify what kind of non-theistic alternative or evidentiary objection would materially defeat the proposed explanation.

routes.description: Show that transcendental facts can be accepted without a demonstrated personal ground and that the proposed divine explanation fails to discriminate among alternatives or meet an adequate public evidentiary standard.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if grounding is not shown necessary, the inference from transcendental facts to a personal God remains underdetermined, and the available observations do not provide sufficiently specific, reliable, or comparative support for the divine hypothesis.

motionBridge.description: Show that transcendental facts do not provide sufficiently discriminating support for a necessary personal God to count as good evidence.

centralBridges.description: Establish that logical truths may hold or describe reality without a further personal or transcendent ontological ground.
Show that consistency with transcendental facts does not establish God as more likely than unexamined or non-theistic alternatives.
Require support that reliably connects the observed facts to a sufficiently specific divine hypothesis and establishes the argument's premises.
Compare the ambiguity and limited public verifiability of the evidence with what a capable personal God could be expected to provide.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why withholding judgment can avoid adding an unevidenced entity when the need for an additional ground is disputed.
Distinguish possible first-person warrant from evidence capable of supporting the divine conclusion for other people.

sections.title: Whether Transcendental Facts Require a Ground
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether the explanatory demand initiating the transcendental argument is warranted or whether logical necessity and practical reliability can stand without an additional metaphysical foundation.

sections.title: From Transcendental Facts to a Necessary Personal Mind
sections.rationale: This section covers the indispensable inferential step from the properties of logic and other abstract truths to mind, personality, necessity, and ultimately the specific kind of God asserted by the motion.

sections.title: Abduction, Alternatives, and Comparative Explanation
sections.rationale: The motion depends on whether the divine account can be compared responsibly with naturalism, Platonism, brute facts, agnosticism, and unspecified alternatives under explanatory-scope and parsimony criteria.

sections.title: Standards for Good Evidence and Sound Inference
sections.rationale: The parties dispute whether philosophical and abductive support can establish the relevant premises or whether reliable, specific, testable, and publicly confirmable support is required for the God hypothesis.

sections.title: Divine Revelation, Hiddenness, and Evidential Expectations
sections.rationale: Claims about what a capable personal God could reveal bear on whether ambiguous transcendental and cumulative evidence fits the hypothesis and on the distinction between private warrant and public support.

routes.description: Establish that mechanistic cosmology does not exhaust the question of existence, then argue that the universe's life-permitting, intelligible, law-governed, and information-bearing character is better accounted for by a fundamental rational mind, with revelation identifying the proposed creator.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the combined case makes divine mind a warranted explanation of why a comprehensible, life-permitting universe exists while answering naturalistic objections from selection effects, physical origin models, cosmic scale, and evidential standards.

motionBridge.description: Connect the universe's existence and salient structure to purposive agency without treating the creator as a substitute for ordinary physical mechanisms.

centralBridges.description: Show that physical accounts of how cosmic states develop leave a distinct burden concerning why any universe, laws, or productive physical states exist.
Show that life-permitting conditions require an explanation not supplied merely by the fact that observers can observe only compatible conditions.
Relate the rational intelligibility, lawfulness, and information-bearing features of nature to a rational source while addressing matter-first alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain why cosmic scale, hostility, and limited biological distribution do not by themselves defeat purposive creation or human significance.
Supply a basis for identifying the proposed creator and defend the admissibility of historical or revelatory evidence alongside evidence from nature.

routes.description: Require independent, testable evidence before inferring cosmic purpose, show that apparent design and intelligibility admit natural or selection-based accounts, and present physical cosmology as capable of explaining the observed universe without requiring divine agency.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if current cosmology and natural processes adequately account for the relevant observations while the proposed purposive inference remains unsupported, presupposes purpose, exceeds the evidence, or depends on prior religious commitments.

motionBridge.description: Establish that the observed universe can be investigated and accounted for through physical processes without evidential need for a divine mind.

centralBridges.description: Require purpose to be independently demonstrated rather than built into why-questions or inferred from humanity's presence in the universe.
Show that observer selection, uncertain possibilities for life, and non-optimal cosmic conditions block a necessary inference from fine-tuning to design.
Provide a physically coherent account under which a universe may arise without a prior universe and clarify the physical senses assigned to nothing.
Apply observational, testable, and falsifiable standards to cosmological and supernatural claims without relying on personal authority.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Explain reliable human reasoning and comprehension through evolved physical minds whose predictions are checked against observation.
Examine whether revelation, miracle claims, historical documents, and antecedent religious commitments independently support the cosmological inference.

sections.title: Existence, Nothing, and the Reach of Physical Cosmology
sections.rationale: This issue bears directly on whether a physical account of cosmic emergence answers the motion or leaves a further explanatory burden concerning why any universe, laws, or physical states exist.

sections.title: Fine-Tuning, Selection Effects, and Life-Permitting Conditions
sections.rationale: The design inference depends substantially on whether life-compatible parameters demand purposive explanation or are adequately addressed by observer selection, alternative possibilities, and the universe's limited hospitality to life.

sections.title: Cosmic Intelligibility, Natural Law, and Information
sections.rationale: This section tests whether rational comprehensibility, dependable cognition, law-governed order, and biological information support mind as fundamental or remain explicable within a physical evolutionary account.

sections.title: Cosmic Purpose, Scale, and Human Significance
sections.rationale: Claims about purpose must address whether cosmic vastness, hostility, inefficiency, and the distribution of life undermine human-centered design or are compatible with value that is not measured by physical scale.

sections.title: Standards of Evidence, Revelation, and Supernatural Claims
sections.rationale: The competing accounts rely on different views of admissible evidence, making testability, miracles, historical documents, scientific authority, revelation, and prior commitments material to whether either worldview is supported.
